260.title: One dark night
260.hook: his poem: a soul slips out of the sleeping house to meet her beloved
260.carry: my house being now at rest
260.howItsDone: Catholics read John's poem The Dark Night and his commentaries on it, often with a spiritual director, to understand seasons when prayer and faith feel dark, and Carmelites pray and sing his poems.

screen: `DAY TWO-HUNDRED-SIXTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the escape: a rope of blankets, a fall, and nuns who hid him. Your line was out the window. What screw did you loosen? Today, the poem that came out of all that darkness. Day two hundred sixty.
screen: `OUT THE WINDOW.`

segments.voice: You've heard the phrase. Someone's going through a dark night of the soul. People use it for burnout, a breakup, a bad year, a crisis of faith. It's on book covers and in song lyrics. Almost nobody who says it knows where it comes from. It comes from a poem of eight short stanzas, written by a small, thin friar not long after he climbed out of a prison window. And the surprise is this: it isn't a sad poem. It's a love poem. Today's word is its night.
screen: `A DARK NIGHT OF THE SOUL.` → `FROM EIGHT SHORT STANZAS.` → `NOT A SAD POEM. A LOVE POEM.`

segments.voice: First, the story. The poem begins, in John's Spanish: "En una noche oscura," on a dark night. A young woman, burning with love, slips out of her house while everyone is asleep. She goes, as the first stanza ends, "estando ya mi casa sosegada," my house being now at rest. Nobody sees her. She takes a secret stair. She's in disguise. She carries no light at all, except the one burning in her heart, and that light, she says, guides her more surely than the noonday sun, to the place where her beloved is waiting. Second, who's who. For John, the young woman is the soul, and the beloved is God. The sleeping house is everything in us that usually runs the show: our appetites, our worries, our need to control. When the house finally goes quiet, the soul can slip out to meet God. Third, the turn. Then comes the line people remember. Oh night that guided me, she sings, oh night more lovely than the dawn. The darkness isn't the enemy. It's what got her there. Without the dark, she'd never have slipped out unseen. Fourth, the books. John knew his poem needed explaining, so he wrote two whole books about it, the Ascent of Mount Carmel and the Dark Night. In them, the night becomes a way of describing how God leads a soul through times when the old lights go out. Over the next days we'll walk through those books. But start here, with the poem: a night that's also a love story.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit in the dark for two minutes. Turn off the light if you can, or close your eyes and cover them with your hands. Let the house of you go quiet: the lists, the plans, the noise. Don't look for anything. Just notice that the dark isn't empty. If you pray, you can wait for God there, the way the young woman went out to meet her beloved. If you don't, let the dark be a place to rest. The bell holds the time.
Dark night. From John of the Cross's poem: the night in which the soul, its house at rest, slips out to meet God. Not despair, but a love story. Today's word.

261.title: The night of the senses
261.hook: when prayer stops feeling good, God may be weaning us from the sweets
261.howItsDone: Catholic spiritual directors often turn to John's Dark Night, book one, when people say prayer has gone dry, and encourage them to keep praying faithfully rather than chasing feelings.

screen: `DAY TWO-HUNDRED-SIXTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dark night: a love poem, a sleeping house, a soul slipping out to meet God. Your line was my house being now at rest. Did you sit a minute in the dark? Today, John explains the first part of that night. Day two hundred sixty-one.
screen: `MY HOUSE BEING NOW AT REST.`

segments.voice: Here's something people who pray don't always say out loud. At the start, it can feel wonderful. You go to Mass, or sit in a quiet church, or read a psalm, and you feel something warm. Tears, sometimes. Peace. You can't wait to go back. And then one day, it's just gone. You show up. You say the words. Nothing. Flat as cardboard. Most people assume they've done something wrong, or that God has left, or that it was never real. John of the Cross had a very different explanation.
screen: `AT FIRST, IT FEELS WONDERFUL.` → `THEN ONE DAY, NOTHING.` → `DID GOD LEAVE?`

segments.voice: First, the mother. John opens his book the Dark Night with a picture everyone knows. A loving mother holds her baby close, warms it, and feeds it with sweet milk. That's how God treats beginners in prayer, he says: with comfort and sweetness. Second, the weaning. But a mother who loves her child doesn't nurse it forever. The day comes when she weans it. She sets it down so it will learn to walk, and it cries, because it wants the milk. Saint Paul says something similar to one young church, in the Douay-Rheims: "I gave you milk to drink, not meat; for you were not able as yet." John says God does the same with souls. The sweetness is taken away, not to punish, but so they can grow. Third, the sweet tooth. John is funny and sharp about beginners. He lists their faults in prayer: wanting more and more good feelings, like a spiritual sweet tooth; judging others who seem less devout; getting sulky when prayer is dull. The night of the senses, he says, is God's cure for all that. When the feelings dry up, you find out whether you were seeking God, or the sweets God gave. Fourth, dry is not gone. That's the heart of it. Dryness in prayer, John says, is often a sign that God is closer, not farther. It's God doing the work now, quietly, below what you can feel. He doesn't say every dry spell is this. Tomorrow he'll give us ways to tell. But he says: don't assume God left because the sweetness did.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray today even if it's dry. Sit, and breathe. Don't try to make anything happen. If you pray, just be with God for these two minutes, even if it feels like talking to a wall. That counts. If you don't pray, sit with something you've been faithful to that doesn't feel exciting anymore, a friendship, a job, a promise, and notice that showing up still matters. The bell holds the time.
The night of the senses. John's name for the time when the sweetness of prayer dries up, as God weans a soul from comfort so it can grow. Today's word.

262.title: Three signs (Dark Night 1.9)
262.hook: no taste for things, no ease in meditation, yet a quiet wish for God
262.howItsDone: Catholic spiritual directors use John's three signs (Dark Night 1.9) to help people discern dryness in prayer, and often also ask about sleep, health and mood, recommending medical or counseling help when needed.

screen: `DAY TWO-HUNDRED-SIXTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the night of the senses, when God weans a soul from the sweets. Your line was dry is not gone. What faithful thing did you do that didn't feel like anything? Today, how John says to tell. Day two hundred sixty-two.
screen: `DRY IS NOT GONE.`

segments.voice: A dry patch in prayer can come from a lot of places. Maybe you've drifted, and stopped caring. Maybe you're exhausted, or sick, or haven't slept in weeks. Maybe something heavier is going on, a depression that makes everything gray, not just prayer. Or maybe it's what John of the Cross called the night of the senses, God quietly at work. From the inside, they can all feel the same. So John, who was a careful teacher and a good spiritual director, gave three signs to tell them apart. Today's word is those signs.
screen: `DRIFTING? TIRED? DEPRESSED?` → `OR GOD AT WORK?` → `FROM THE INSIDE, THE SAME.`

segments.voice: They're in the Dark Night, book one, chapter nine. First sign: no taste for anything. Prayer has lost its sweetness. But so has everything else you might run to instead. It isn't that you've swapped God for something shinier. Nothing much satisfies. John says that matters: if you'd simply drifted, you'd be enjoying something else. Second sign: the quiet wish. This is the key. Even in the dryness, your mind keeps turning to God, with a painful kind of care. You worry that you're not serving God, that you're going backward. John says that very worry is a good sign. Someone who had truly stopped caring wouldn't worry at all. The longing stays, even when the feelings go. Third sign: meditation won't work anymore. The old way of praying, thinking through a Gospel scene, picturing it, working at it, just won't go. You try, and your mind slides off. John says this is because God is beginning to give himself in a quieter, simpler way, beneath thinking. So don't strain at the old methods. Rest, quietly and lovingly. Fourth, an honest caution. John himself says dryness can also come from what he calls melancholy, from the body, and that it's different: the quiet longing for God is missing. Today we'd say plainly, if a heaviness is sitting on everything, sleep, food, work, joy, not just prayer, talk to a doctor or a counselor. Many Catholic spiritual directors say the same. Grace and good care aren't rivals.
screen: `ONE: NO TASTE FOR ANYTHING.` · `TWO: THE QUIET WISH FOR GOD.` · `THREE: MEDITATION WON'T GO.` · `A CAUTION: CARE FOR THE BODY TOO.` · then, large: `THE LONGING STAYS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask gently which you feel. Settle and breathe. Without judging yourself, ask: what's prayer like for me right now? Sweet, flat, or somewhere between? Do other things feel flat too? Is there still a quiet wish underneath, for God or for something good? There are no wrong answers. If you pray, you can tell God what you find. If you don't, just notice. And if something heavy is there, let this be the moment you decide to tell someone. The bell holds the time.
Three signs. John's way to recognize the night of the senses: no taste for anything, a quiet, anxious wish for God, and meditation that won't go. Today's word.

263.title: The night of the spirit
263.hook: a deeper night, where even our ideas of God are purified
263.howItsDone: Catholics who experience long seasons of spiritual darkness are often pointed to the second book of John's Dark Night, usually with an experienced spiritual director, and the Church remembers saints such as Thérèse of Lisieux who described similar nights.

screen: `DAY TWO-HUNDRED-SIXTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, three signs to tell the night of the senses from drifting or illness. Your line was the longing stays. Did you find the wish underneath the flat? Today, John says there's a second, deeper night. Day two hundred sixty-three.
screen: `THE LONGING STAYS.`

segments.voice: Think about the picture of God you had at seven years old. For a lot of people it's a kind old man on a cloud. Or a stern one. Maybe a very large grandfather, or a referee with a whistle. Most of us grow out of that one. But John of the Cross says we keep carrying pictures of God around, grown-up ones: God as my cheerleader, God as a rule book, God as the one who'll make my life work out. And he says there's a night in which even those get taken away. Today's word is that night.
screen: `A MAN ON A CLOUD.` → `GROWN-UP PICTURES OF GOD.` → `A NIGHT THAT TAKES THEM AWAY.`

segments.voice: First, who it's for. John says the night of the senses is common, and the night of the spirit is for fewer people, those who have already come a long way in prayer. It goes deeper. The first night weaned us from sweet feelings. This one reaches our understanding, our memory and our will, the very ways we think about God. Second, the ray of darkness. John borrows an image from an older Christian writer. Look straight at the sun, and what do you see? Nothing. You're blinded. Not because there's too little light, but too much. So when God comes very close to a soul, John says, it feels like darkness. He calls it a ray of darkness. Third, the pain. John doesn't soften this. People in this night can feel abandoned, dry, even rejected by God, like the writer of Lamentations sitting in the ruins. Their old ideas of God don't hold up anymore, and nothing has taken their place yet. It's frightening. John says it's also love: God is making room for himself, the real God, not our picture. Fourth, bigger than your idea. The prophet Isaiah hears God say, in the Douay-Rheims: "For my thoughts are not your thoughts: nor your ways my ways, saith the Lord." John says any idea of God we can hold in our heads is smaller than God. That doesn't make the ideas useless. The Church's teaching still stands. But the God it points to is always larger. Losing a picture, for John, isn't losing God. It can be finding him.
screen: `A DEEPER NIGHT, FOR FEWER.` · `A RAY OF DARKNESS.` · `THE OLD PICTURES DON'T HOLD.` · `GOD IS ALWAYS LARGER.` · then, large: `MY THOUGHTS ARE NOT YOUR THOUGHTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let go of one fixed picture of God. Settle and breathe. Notice one picture of God you carry: the referee, the distant boss, the one who's disappointed in you, the one who owes you a good life. Just see it. Then, gently, set it down. Don't rush to replace it. If you pray, you can simply say, you're more than this. If you don't, try holding the idea that whatever is deepest is larger than your picture of it. The bell holds the time.
The night of the spirit. John's deeper night, where even our ideas of God are purified, and God's nearness can feel like darkness. Today's word.
screen: `THE NIGHT OF THE SPIRIT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: bigger than your idea. Today, when you catch yourself sure you know exactly what God, or anyone, is like, add the words: and more than that. Day two hundred sixty-three.

264.title: Nada (Ascent of Mount Carmel)
264.hook: his drawing of the mountain: nothing, nothing, nothing, and on the mountain, nothing
264.howItsDone: Carmelites and many Catholics study John's sketch of Mount Carmel and the nada verses from the Ascent, often as a guide to detachment in Lent or on retreat.

screen: `DAY TWO-HUNDRED-SIXTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the night of the spirit, where even our ideas of God are purified. Your line was bigger than your idea. Did you add and more than that? Today, one small Spanish word, drawn on a mountain. Day two hundred sixty-four.
screen: `BIGGER THAN YOUR IDEA.`

segments.voice: After his escape, John was sent south, and for a while he often visited a convent of Carmelite nuns in the town of Beas. He was their confessor and teacher. One day he did something teachers still do. He sat down and drew them a diagram. A mountain. Paths winding up it. Words written along the paths. He made copies and handed them out, so each nun could keep one in her breviary. The drawing still exists, in early copies. And written again and again up the middle path is today's word.
screen: `A CONVENT IN BEAS.` → `A TEACHER DRAWS A DIAGRAM.` → `A MOUNTAIN WITH WORDS ON IT.`

segments.voice: First, the two wide roads. On the left and right of John's mountain are broad paths. One is labeled with the goods of earth: possessions, pleasure, knowledge, comfort. The other with the goods of heaven: glory, joy, consolation, even spiritual rewards. Both look sensible. Both wind around and stop short. They don't reach the top. Second, the narrow way. Straight up the middle is a thin path. And on it John writes one Spanish word, over and over: nada, nada, nada, nada. Nothing. And near the top: and even on the mountain, nothing. Third, the verses. Beside the drawing, and later in his book the Ascent of Mount Carmel, John writes lines that turn on this word. In his Spanish: "Para venir a gustarlo todo, no quieras tener gusto en nada." To come to enjoy everything, desire to have enjoyment in nothing. Then: to come to possess everything, desire to possess nothing. To come to be everything, desire to be nothing. Fourth, what it means. This sounds bleak. It isn't meant to be. John isn't saying the world is bad, or that people don't matter. He loved the countryside, and his friends. His point is about grasping. If you cling to anything, even good things, even spiritual things, your hands are full. Nada is emptying the hands. And the promise at the top of the drawing is not nothing. It's everything, which is God. The whole word is nothing, then everything. Only the order matters.
screen: `TWO WIDE ROADS STOP SHORT.` · `NADA, NADA, NADA UP THE MIDDLE.` · `TO ENJOY ALL, CLING TO NOTHING.` · `EMPTY HANDS, THEN EVERYTHING.` · then, large: `NO QUIERAS TENER GUSTO EN NADA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: want one thing less today. Settle and breathe. Open your hands on your knees, palms up. Think of one thing you've been wanting hard, a purchase, a result, someone's approval, even a certain feeling in prayer. Picture it in your open hands. Now let it rest there without gripping. You don't have to throw it away. Just stop clutching. If you pray, you can offer it to God. If you don't, notice how open hands feel. The bell holds the time.
Nada. Spanish for nothing, written up the narrow path on John's drawing of Mount Carmel: cling to nothing, and at the top, God, who is everything. Today's word.

265.title: The bird on a thread (Ascent 1.11)
265.hook: a bird tied by a thin thread can't fly any more than one tied by a cord
265.howItsDone: Catholics often use John's bird-on-a-thread image in examinations of conscience and Lenten practices, looking for small voluntary attachments rather than only for large sins.

screen: `DAY TWO-HUNDRED-SIXTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, nada: nothing, nothing, nothing up the narrow path. Your line was nothing, then everything. What did you skip, and how did the empty space feel? Today, one of John's simplest pictures. Day two hundred sixty-five.
screen: `NOTHING, THEN EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: Most of us are pretty sure we're not attached to much. We're not addicts. We're not greedy. Sure, there's the phone we check a hundred times a day. The grudge against that one cousin. The need to be right in the group chat. The show we have to finish. The little bit of pride about how we look, or how busy we are. But those are small. Harmless. Thin little threads, really. John of the Cross has a picture for exactly those small things. Today's word is that picture.
screen: `NOT ATTACHED TO MUCH.` → `EXCEPT A FEW SMALL THINGS.` → `THIN LITTLE THREADS.`

segments.voice: First, the bird. In the Ascent of Mount Carmel, John says: it makes little difference whether a bird is tied by a thin thread or a thick cord. Either way, it can't fly. Sure, the thread is easier to break. But until it's broken, the bird is held just as firmly as if it were tied with rope. Second, what counts as a thread. John is specific, and surprisingly ordinary. He mentions being attached to a person, to a piece of clothing, a book, a room, a certain kind of food, a bit of gossip, a small pleasure in knowing things. None of these are sins in themselves. What matters, he says, is the voluntary clinging, the grip we choose and keep choosing. He's not talking about the natural wants everyone has, which come and go on their own. He means the ones we hold on to. Third, the little fish. He adds another picture. Sailors in his day told of a tiny fish, the remora, that could fasten itself to a great ship and slow it down. Small thing, big ship. The size of the attachment isn't the point. The holding is. Fourth, why he cares. It's not that John wants us miserable. It's that he's seen so many people who have given up enormous things, left home, joined monasteries, and then got stuck for years on something tiny. A favorite cup. A grudge. It breaks his heart a little, because they were so close to flying. Just one thread. And the good news hiding in the image is this: a thread is the easiest thing in the world to cut.
screen: `A THREAD OR A CORD, NO FLIGHT.` · `A BOOK, A ROOM, A BIT OF GOSSIP.` · `A LITTLE FISH HOLDS A SHIP.` · `SO CLOSE TO FLYING.` · then, large: `A THREAD STILL HOLDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one thin thread. Settle and breathe. Ask yourself, honestly and without shame, what small thing has a grip on you? Not the big obvious ones. The little one you'd never mention. A habit, a comfort, a grudge, a need to be noticed. Let it come to mind. Name it, quietly, in one word. If you pray, you can show it to God and ask for help to cut it. If you don't, just picture the thread, and the scissors. The bell holds the time.
The bird on a thread. John's picture in the Ascent: a bird tied by a thin thread can't fly any more than one tied by a cord. Today's word.
screen: `THE BIRD ON A THREAD — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: a thread still holds. Today, cut your thread for one day: skip the habit, drop the grudge, let someone else be right. Day two hundred sixty-five.

266.title: Faith as a dark light (Ascent 2)
266.hook: faith guides like a light we can't look at directly
266.howItsDone: Catholics describe faith as trust in what God has revealed rather than in what they can see or prove, and spiritual directors in the Carmelite tradition steer people away from seeking visions toward plain faith.

screen: `DAY TWO-HUNDRED-SIXTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bird on a thread: a thin thread holds as well as a cord. Your line was a thread still holds. Which thread did you cut? Today, how John says we find our way in the dark. Day two hundred sixty-six.
screen: `A THREAD STILL HOLDS.`

segments.voice: Try looking straight at the sun at noon. You can't, not for more than a blink. It's the brightest thing in the sky, and it's the one thing you can't see. And yet everything else you see today, you'll see because of it. The trees, the faces, the words on this screen. You don't look at the sun. You look by it. John of the Cross says faith works like that. It's a light. But it's a light that feels, from the inside, like darkness. Today's word is that strange light.
screen: `YOU CAN'T LOOK AT THE SUN.` → `YOU SEE EVERYTHING BY IT.` → `A LIGHT THAT FEELS LIKE DARK.`

segments.voice: First, a dark night. In the second book of the Ascent, John calls faith itself a dark night for the soul. Faith, he says, asks us to trust what we can't see, touch or prove, on the word of God. That's dark to the mind, which wants to see for itself. But he adds: the darker it is for the mind, the more light it gives the soul. Second, the cloud. John points to the Exodus story. As Israel escapes Egypt, a pillar of cloud stands between them and the army chasing them. The Douay-Rheims says: "it was a dark cloud, and enlightening the night." Dark on one side, light on the other. The same cloud. John says that's faith: darkness to our understanding, light for our way. Third, the walk. Saint Paul says, in the Douay-Rheims: "For we walk by faith, and not by sight." Walking isn't the same as understanding. You can walk a path you can't see the end of, one step, in trust. Fourth, why not visions? John warns people not to chase visions, voices and special signs. They can be misleading, he says, and even true ones can become something to cling to. Faith is the surer guide, precisely because it's plain, humble and dark. Look back at this week: one dark night, a love poem. The night of the senses, dry is not gone. Three signs. The night of the spirit, bigger than your idea. Nada. A bird on a thread. And today, the light we can't look at but see by. It's all one night.
screen: `FAITH IS DARK TO THE MIND.` · `A DARK CLOUD THAT LIGHTS THE NIGHT.` · `WALKING, NOT SEEING.` · `DON'T CHASE VISIONS.` · then, large: `FOR WE WALK BY FAITH, AND NOT BY SIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: trust one thing you can't see. Settle and breathe. Think of something in your life that's unresolved, where you can't see the end. A diagnosis, a job, a child's choices, a question about God. Don't try to solve it. Picture it as a path in the dark, and yourself taking just one step. If you pray, you can hand the unseen part to God and ask only for the next step. If you don't, name the one step you can see. The bell holds the time.
Faith as a dark light. John's teaching in the Ascent: faith is dark to the mind, like a cloud, and yet it lights the way. Today's word.
screen: `FAITH AS A DARK LIGHT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: walk by faith. Today, take the one step you can see, and leave the rest of the path for later. Day two hundred sixty-six.

screen: `DAY 266 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHERE HAVE YOU HIDDEN.`
